subject: literacy
title: Long a with ai and ay

activities.title: Long a with ai and ay
parentPrompts: Write "rain" and "play." Say each word and point out that ai and ay both make the long a sound. Tell your child that ai is usually in the middle of a word and ay is usually at the end.
Read these lists aloud together: ai (rain, mail, tail, snail, paint), ay (day, play, tray, stay, say).
Say a word and your child writes it with the right spelling: wait, gray, pay, train, away, braid. Use one color for ai and another for ay.
Make up a silly sentence together that uses at least two of the words, then write it. Check: they spell most ai/ay words correctly and can read all the words in the lists.

subject: literacy
title: Long e with ee and ea

activities.title: Long e with ee and ea
parentPrompts: Write "seed" and "leaf." Say both and explain that ee and ea can both say long e.
Read together: ee (feet, tree, green, sleep, jeep) and ea (team, beach, bean, read, meat). Note that ea can also say short e in a few words like "bread" and "head."

Write 8 words on cards, each missing the vowel team (for example: s__d, b__ch, tr__, gr__n). Your child fills in ee or ea and reads the word. More than one answer may fit a few, so ask them which one makes a real word.
Have your child write two sentences using one ee word and one ea word. Check: they can read the words in each group and know a few words where ea sounds different.

subject: literacy
title: Long o with oa and ow

activities.title: Long o with oa and ow
materials: a small object like a toy boat (optional)
parentPrompts: Write "boat" and "snow." Say them and ask what sound they share in the middle or end. (Both have long o.)
Read these together: oa (coat, road, toast, soap, goat) and ow (show, grow, slow, window, yellow). Mention that ow can also say the sound in "cow," so they should try both and see which makes sense.
Play "I spy a word": say a clue ("Something you wear when it is cold" - coat; "What a seed does" - grow). Your child writes the answer.
Together, write a 3-line silly rhyme using oa or ow words, such as "A goat in a coat sailed in a boat." Check: they can read the words and use the right oa/ow pattern.

activities.title: Read it like a character
materials: a favorite picture book with dialogue
parentPrompts: Choose a page of dialogue from a book you both like. Read a short part aloud with a big expressive voice, then read it flat and boring. Ask: "Which was better, and why?"
Look at the punctuation: a period means stop, a question mark means your voice goes up, and an exclamation point means show strong feeling. Practice with: "We won!" "Where is my hat?" "I am tired."
Take turns: you read one character's words and your child reads another, using a different voice for each.
Ask your child to reread one page twice. Check: their voice changes for questions and exclamations, and they use different voices for different characters.

activities.title: My opinion and why
parentPrompts: Ask: "What is the best snack, game, or animal, in your opinion?" Explain that an opinion is what someone thinks or feels, and a fact can be checked.
Practice sorting by saying statements. "Cats have fur" (fact) and "Cats are the best pets" (opinion). Do 4 or 5 quick rounds.

Have your child write: one sentence that names the topic, one sentence that states their opinion, and one sentence with a reason that starts with "because." For example: "I want to tell you about swimming. Swimming is the best sport. I think so because it is cool on a hot day."
Read it aloud. Check: the writing states an opinion and gives at least one reason using the word "because." Celebrate any reason that makes sense to the writer.

activities.title: Ten tens make a hundred
materials: 100 small objects (beans, dry pasta, or paper squares)
parentPrompts: Count out 10 objects into a cup. Make 10 cups. Ask: "How many are in each cup? How many cups?"
Count by tens to 100 as you point to each cup. Say: "Ten tens make one hundred."
Write 100 and show it as a bundle of ten tens. Then show 30 as 3 tens and 60 as 6 tens.
Ask: "How many tens in 40? 70? 100?" Check: they know that 10 tens equal 100.

activities.title: Hundreds, tens, and ones
materials: base-ten blocks, or paper squares: 1 flat for hundreds, strips for tens, small squares for ones
parentPrompts: If you do not have blocks, draw a big square for 100, a long strip for 10, and a small square for 1.
Build 243 with 2 hundreds, 4 tens, and 3 ones. Ask your child to say the number, then write it.
Build other numbers like 305, 120, and 418. Have your child say how many hundreds, tens, and ones are in each.
Ask: "In 305, what does the 0 mean?" (No tens.) Check: they can explain the value of each digit.

activities.title: Skip count by 5s, 10s, and 100s
parentPrompts: Count by 5s to 100 together while tapping a drum or clapping. Do the same by 10s.
Write the counting numbers on a number path with your child: 5, 10, 15, ... and 10, 20, 30, ... Color them different colors on a hundred chart if you have one.
Count by 100s from 100 to 1000. Ask: "How many tens in 100? How many hundreds in 1000?"
Play "what comes next?": say a skip count (for example: 35, 40, 45, ...) and your child continues. Check: they can skip count without stopping.

subject: math
title: Numbers in words and expanded form

activities.title: Numbers in words and expanded form
parentPrompts: Write 462 and say it: "four hundred sixty-two." Then write it in expanded form: 400 + 60 + 2.
Have your child write 3 numbers (for example, 238, 705, 910) with number names and expanded form.
Play "say it, write it": you say a number to 1000 and your child writes it with digits.
Ask: "What is the same in 462 and 400 + 60 + 2?" Check: they match digit form, number name, and expanded form.

activities.title: Rows and columns
parentPrompts: Show an array of 3 rows with 4 in each row. Ask: "How many in all?" Count by rows: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Build arrays with up to 5 rows and 5 columns. Have your child write a repeated addition sentence for each one.
Find arrays in real life: muffin tins, egg cartons, window panes, a tile floor. Count how many in all.
Ask: "Which arrays have an even number? How do you know?" Check: they use repeated addition to find the total.

activities.title: Stretchy, bendy, and strong
parentPrompts: Gather several materials and discuss what could be tested: stretch, bend, or strength.
Test each material by gently stretching and bending, and record what you see.
Make a chart with columns for each property. Mark a check when the material has that property.
Ask: "Which material would make a good bracelet?" Check: they can match properties to uses.

activities.title: Design a rain hat test
materials: small scraps of materials (cloth, plastic bag, paper, foil)
parentPrompts: Ask: "What would keep a doll dry in the rain?" Make a list of possible materials.
Place each material over a cup and pour 2 spoons of water on top. Watch whether water goes through.
Record which material kept the cup dry. Test again to see if the results are the same.
Ask: "Which material is best for a rain hat? What evidence do you have?" Check: they cite test results.

subject: science
title: Build it, take it apart, build again

activities.title: Build it, take it apart, build again
materials: a set of 12 to 20 building blocks, paper cups or cardboard pieces
parentPrompts: Tell your child that a small set of pieces can build many different things.
Use all the pieces to build something like a tower. Draw it. Take it apart.
Use the same pieces to build something new, such as a bridge or a house. Draw it too.
Ask: "What is the same? What is different?" Check: they say the same pieces made different objects.

activities.title: North, south, east, west
materials: a compass or a compass app (optional)
parentPrompts: Explain that north, south, east, and west are directions that help us say where things are. On most maps, north is at the top.
Draw a compass rose on paper with N at the top, S at the bottom, E on the right, and W on the left.
Label the four walls of a room N, S, E, and W with sticky notes. Play "walk north" and "turn east" together.
Check: they can say which direction something is in on a map, such as "The pond is east of the house."

activities.title: Our neighborhood map
parentPrompts: Talk about the places near home: a park, a store, a library, a school, a road. Choose 5 to 6.
Draw a simple map of your block or street with those places. Add a compass rose and a key.
Ask: "What is next to the park? Which way would you walk to the library?" Use north, south, east, and west if you know them.
Check: they draw places in a sensible spot and explain a path between two of them.
